task_1.diagnosis: The shared histogram increments are read-modify-write operations, so two threads can read the same old value and overwrite each other's updates. An atomic integer increment would protect the count but would not make floating-point addition associative. Different thread schedules and partition sizes change the order of floating-point additions and their rounding. Private rows remove shared writes, and the exact two-limb integer accumulator preserves all binary64 weight units without overflow for this input. Merging the rows in thread-ID order and rounding once gives bit-identical weighted sums at every required thread count.

task_2.diagnosis: Under MESI-style coherence, writing a cache line requires exclusive ownership. Adjacent int64 counters can occupy the same 64-byte line, so otherwise independent writers repeatedly invalidate each other's copies. This is false sharing, not an update race on the same counter. Padding separates active slots by at least 64 bytes, reducing ownership transfers on 64-byte-line CPUs. Both kernels perform a volatile memory update on every iteration to prevent compiler register promotion from hiding the effect. The benchmark keeps work per thread constant, so its times are weak-scaling times; the eight-thread padded/unpadded comparison measures the padding benefit. Hardware with larger coherence lines may exhibit a different benefit from the assigned stride.

task_3.diagnosis: Static prange gives contiguous ranges to workers and can leave a barrier waiting for the most expensive range. The specified modulo workload is periodic, so static scheduling can already be close to balanced for this ID. The balanced scheduler sorts rows by cost and snake-interleaves them into small batches of at most 16 rows with similar operation counts. Each worker claims its next batch through an atomic fetch-add on a shared cursor; no Python lock or static chunk ownership is used. Equal batch quotas limit monopolization, and each row is evaluated exactly once using the same score formula as the static kernel. Load balance is validated by actual per-worker operation counts, separately from elapsed time and scheduling overhead.
